primary_cause: No clear company-specific negative headline. Cancelled in-person Google Cloud Next event. Broad market selloff tied to COVID escalation and oil shock
secondary_factors: Investor concern that travel and brand advertisers would cut spend which later did happen at Alphabet in mid-March
store_description: GOOG's decline looks mostly macro-driven rather than headline-driven. In the prior week Google had already scrapped the physical Cloud Next conference and investors likely began pricing in ad weakness from travel and brand advertisers as COVID spread but on March 9 the overwhelming trigger was the marketwide panic.

primary_cause: COVID-driven fear of sharp auto demand downturn. Reuters Mar 9 reported analysts warning about U.S. auto sales slowdown from coronavirus
secondary_factors: Cyclical and industrial exposure and recession fears amplified by Crash Monday
store_description: GM's 13.9% drop was steeper than the index because autos were immediately viewed as recession-sensitive discretionary purchases. On March 9 Reuters noted analysts were already warning about a showroom sales slowdown from coronavirus layered on top of the marketwide oil-and-COVID panic.

primary_cause: No material negative Gilead-specific headline. Remdesivir story still speculative positive and uncertain. Broad market liquidation on Crash Monday
secondary_factors: Profit-taking after earlier remdesivir enthusiasm and uncertainty about whether the drug would work
store_description: Gilead's fall appears to have been mostly market beta rather than a company-specific disappointment. Investors knew remdesivir was a possible COVID therapy but there was no decisive positive clinical readout yet so the stock still traded with the broader risk-off tape on Crash Monday.

primary_cause: Combined shock to GE aviation and energy businesses from COVID and oil-price war. Aviation threatened by collapsing travel. Energy hit by 25%+ crude plunge
secondary_factors: Balance-sheet sensitivity and GE reputation as higher-risk industrial at the time
store_description: GE's 12.7% drop was bigger than the index because the March 9 shock hit both of its vulnerable end markets at once. A collapse in global travel threatened GE Aviation while a 25%+ plunge in crude signaled weaker demand and capital spending across energy.

primary_cause: Broad COVID and recession selloff with special concern around Gulfstream and business aviation exposure
secondary_factors: General industrial and defense de-risking and fears of delays to high-ticket aerospace demand. No major negative company-specific headline
store_description: GD's defense business was relatively stable but the market was likely marking down Gulfstream exposure as travel restrictions and recession fears accelerated. No discrete negative news release in the prior 3 days so the best explanation is a macro-led repricing of business-jet demand.

primary_cause: No company-specific negative warning. Honeywell reaffirmed Q1 and full-year forecasts the next day Mar 10. Broad market selloff hitting cyclical industrials
secondary_factors: Exposure to aerospace manufacturing and energy end markets
store_description: HON looks like a cyclical-industrial sympathy sell rather than a stock with its own bad headline. The fact that Honeywell reaffirmed guidance the next day suggests investors were selling first on macro recession fears and exposure to industrial demand not reacting to a fresh company warning.

primary_cause: Oil-price-war shock crushing expectations for energy and industrial capital spending. Highly exposed to oil gas process automation and industrial capex
secondary_factors: General recession fears and Emerson cyclical industrial profile. No discrete Emerson-specific negative release
store_description: EMR's 19% drop is one of the clearest oil-beta reactions even though Emerson is not itself an oil producer. With crude down roughly 25-33% in a day investors rapidly repriced automation and process-equipment demand from energy customers producing a much sharper selloff than the broad market.

primary_cause: Anticipation of severe global shipping and trade disruption from COVID. Directly exposed to global trade and transport disruption
secondary_factors: General recession fears and industrial and e-commerce uncertainty. Reuters later suspended FedEx FY2020 outlook citing significant impact of coronavirus
store_description: FedEx sold off because the market initially viewed the company through the lens of collapsing international commerce disrupted B2B volumes and economic slowdown not yet as an eventual e-commerce beneficiary. The later formal withdrawal of guidance fits the concerns investors were discounting.

primary_cause: No material Salesforce-specific negative headline. Broad risk-off move in high-multiple software
secondary_factors: Concern that enterprise deal cycles and sales execution could slow amid COVID disruption
store_description: CRM appears to have fallen with the market rather than on a company event. On March 9 investors were indiscriminately cutting economically sensitive and higher-valuation names and enterprise software was not yet seen as fully insulated from a sudden halt in corporate spending.

primary_cause: Broad tech selloff plus COVID-related concerns about networking demand and events. Had already withdrawn from Mobile World Congress over coronavirus
secondary_factors: Exposure to enterprise and carrier spending if budgets froze
store_description: Cisco's decline was milder than many cyclicals but there was a clear COVID context because it had pulled out of Mobile World Congress. The main driver was still the broad crash with enterprise-tech caution as an extra headwind.

primary_cause: Broad market decline. CVS announced Mar 6 COVID-19 resources for Aetna members including no-copay diagnostic testing and telemedicine
secondary_factors: Worries about near-term healthcare costs utilization shifts and insurance and pharmacy margin uncertainty
store_description: CVS was relatively defensive so a 4.4% drop likely reflects market stress more than company-specific damage. The March 6 Aetna announcement showed management already moving to absorb some COVID-related costs which may have added a small uncertainty discount on top of the broader selloff.

primary_cause: Broad market liquidation not company-specific bad news. Small 3.0% drop much less than market
secondary_factors: Investors balancing near-term stockpiling benefits against logistics pressure and general equity de-risking. Reuters later described widespread panic buying at Costco
store_description: Costco's small 3.0% drop much less than the market is a sign investors already viewed it as relatively resilient. No negative company-specific news in the 3 days before the drop. The surrounding news flow pointed to panic buying which likely cushioned the decline rather than caused it.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Deere warned with Feb 21 earnings that coronavirus would hit Q2 sales and earnings even as it posted unexpected profit increase
secondary_factors: Crash Monday recession fears and cyclical industrial exposure
store_description: Deere's March 9 drop was not just macro noise because the company had already explicitly flagged coronavirus as a second-quarter headwind. Investors were repricing DE with both company guidance risk and the broader economic panic producing a sharper fall than the S&P 500.

primary_cause: No clear negative Danaher-specific headline. Cytiva acquisition still pending closed Mar 31. Broad market and healthcare and industrial de-risking
secondary_factors: Temporary uncertainty around integration and financing and exposure to life-sciences and industrial demand. Smaller drawdown relative to heavy cyclicals
store_description: Danaher's move looks mostly macro-driven. No obvious company-specific negative development just before March 9 and the stock's smaller drawdown relative to heavy cyclicals suggests investors still viewed it as higher quality even while selling almost everything.

primary_cause: COVID threat to parks theatrical releases and travel and leisure demand. Businesses directly exposed — theme parks cruises box office mass gatherings
secondary_factors: General market crash and concern about ESPN and live events. China disruption already hurting film releases. Within days would close major U.S. parks
store_description: Disney was one of the most obviously COVID-exposed media names on March 9 because so much of its business depended on travel and large crowds. Even though the formal U.S. park shutdown announcement came on March 12 investors were already discounting that kind of disruption.

primary_cause: No meaningful Duke-specific negative headline. Broad market selloff. Utilities safer than cyclicals but still fell in circuit-breaker session
secondary_factors: Investors raised cash and lower Treasury yields and defensive positioning were not enough to fully offset indiscriminate selling
store_description: Duke's move appears macro-driven. Utilities were safer than cyclicals that day but they still fell as investors sold across sectors during the circuit-breaker session. No evidence of a Duke-specific operational shock in the March 6-9 window.

primary_cause: Direct hit from Saudi-Russia oil price war. Oil prices biggest daily rout since 1991 Gulf War. Crude down roughly 25% with intraday declines as large as about 33%
secondary_factors: COVID demand destruction and broader equity liquidation
store_description: CVX's 15.4% drop was overwhelmingly oil-specific. The collapse of OPEC+ cooperation and Saudi price cuts caused a historic crude crash just as COVID was destroying fuel demand so integrated oil majors were repriced immediately for lower cash flow and weaker upstream economics.

primary_cause: No material ServiceNow-specific negative. WHO pandemic declaration and Trump European travel restrictions triggered March 11 selloff
secondary_factors: De-rating of high-multiple software amid fears enterprise IT spending and deal timing would deteriorate
store_description: ServiceNow's decline looks macro rather than idiosyncratic. When the WHO declared a pandemic and Trump announced European travel restrictions investors sold richly valued software names on fear that even recurring-revenue enterprise vendors could face slower new bookings and elongated sales cycles.

primary_cause: No significant Merck-specific negative catalyst. Broad market and pandemic selloff on March 11. Modest defensive outperformance — pharma seen as safer
secondary_factors: Relatively small 3.4% decline suggests mostly dragged by market not punished for company news
store_description: Merck's relatively small 3.4% decline suggests it was mostly being dragged by the market not punished for any company news. In the March 8-11 window no fresh Merck-specific disappointment was found and pharma broadly held up better than cyclicals.

primary_cause: No company-specific negative. Marketwide pandemic shock on March 11 after WHO declaration and Trump Europe travel ban
secondary_factors: Stay-at-home winner thesis not yet fully embraced. Production disruption risk existed. Fell less than market
store_description: Netflix fell less than the market because it was already somewhat defensive but on March 11 it still traded in a broad risk-off tape after the WHO pandemic declaration and Trump Europe travel ban. No clear stock-specific bad news so this looks like temporary correlation with the overall panic.
